name: DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization)
primaryDefinition: A collectively-owned organization coordinated by rules encoded in a blockchain's smart contracts rather than a traditional management hierarchy — decisions happen through open proposals and voting, and treasury funds require the group's collective on-chain approval to move.[a]
shortDescription: A collectively owned organization run by rules encoded in smart contracts, with decisions made through open proposals and votes.
governanceModel: Token-based or 1-member-1-vote on-chain voting; proposals executed automatically via smart contract once passed. Decision-making is decentralized (who decides), not necessarily networked (how they coordinate).[b] DAOs can also federate: Kevin Owocki's "DAO of DAOs" describes DAOs interoperating through social, technical and governance layers — a pattern among DAOs rather than a distinct organizational type.[c]
legalTerritorialStatus: No inherent territorial ambition. Legal personhood is typically absent or bolted on separately (e.g. a Wyoming DAO LLC wrapper); operates purely as digital/financial infrastructure.
membershipBasis: Token or NFT holding, or on-chain reputation; membership is fungible/transferable in most token-based DAOs.
fundingTreasury: On-chain treasury (multisig or protocol-controlled), funded by token sales, protocol revenue, or member contributions; fully transparent, proposal-gated spending.
representativeExamples: See the DAO comparison page (linked from this row) for individual examples across governance models, treasuries, and legal wrappers.
differentiationNote: Unlike a Network State or Network Nation, a DAO makes no claim to territory or population scale — it is purely digital/financial infrastructure, governed by on-chain voting rather than shared ideology or values-alignment. Unlike the institutional baselines (nation-state, corporation, nonprofit), its legal personhood is typically absent or bolted on. It is also the only one of these types with its own dedicated entities-comparison page on this site today, cataloging specific real-world DAOs rather than the DAO concept itself.

relatedTechnology.note: A DAO's rules and treasury controls are encoded in blockchain smart contracts, so it needs a platform that can run them; Ethereum, Solana and NEAR are listed as examples.

relatedMechanisms.note: DAOs and ecosystems commonly use quadratic funding to share a grants budget so that broad support counts for more than a few large donors, and Gitcoin's open-source Allo Protocol builds on its experience running 18 such rounds.
Several ecosystem DAOs use retroactive funding to pay for public-goods impact after it is visible, with Optimism's multi-round RetroPGF program the best known.
Several DAOs, such as Giveth, use augmented bonding curves to fund community treasuries, a pattern proven at community scale rather than large scale.
DAO treasuries hold reserve-backed stablecoins as their main low-volatility asset, roughly eight percent of the twenty largest treasuries in a 2023 study that recommended holding more.
Ether is the main non-native asset in DAO treasuries, roughly nine percent of the twenty largest treasuries in a 2023 study, held alongside each DAO's own token.

references.note: ethereum.org — "DAOs": Ethereum Foundation's own definition, source for the primary definition (collective ownership, proposal-and-vote governance, built-in treasuries requiring group approval).
Jur — "Differences Between Network States and DAOs": DAO vs. Network State contrast, source for the decentralized-vs-networked distinction.

P2P Foundation Wiki — "DAO of DAOs": quotes Kevin Owocki's thread describing a DAO of DAOs as an interconnected network of organizations collaborating through three layers (social, technical, governance). The thread itself (x.com, cited on the wiki page) is not machine-readable; read via a local mirror of the wiki, the same way as reference [a] on the cDPO row. Folded into the DAO row, not given its own row, because it describes DAOs relating to one another rather than a separate organizational form.

name: Network State
primaryDefinition: An online community aligned around a shared mission, with enough collective capacity to crowdfund physical territory in multiple locations worldwide and pursue formal diplomatic recognition as a sovereign state from existing governments.[a] Srinivasan frames it as the end of a lifecycle — an online community (a "startup society"), then a network union, then a network archipelago owning physical territory across jurisdictions, then a network state with diplomatic recognition — so those earlier stages are steps toward this same concept, not separate organizational types here.[b][d] A related "network society" framing is a critique of this model rather than a stage of it: it argues for pluralism and participatory governance in place of exit.[d]
shortDescription: An online community that crowdfunds physical territory in several places and seeks diplomatic recognition as a sovereign state.
governanceModel: A 'decentralized startup society' united by shared ideology; can be one-member-one-vote or centralized if members choose. Core principle: exit-based governance — disagreement leads to forking a new network state, not overriding the majority.[b] Critics have proposed reforms to prevent founder overreach as these communities scale — replacing pure coin-based voting with non-transferable citizen identity, and building in 'exit-to-community' mechanisms and formal representation for surrounding host communities.[c]
legalTerritorialStatus: Deliberately non-contiguous distributed physical territory (apartments, neighborhoods, towns worldwide) linked digitally, explicitly working toward eventual sovereign diplomatic recognition — the defining goal separating it from a DAO or Network Nation. No network state has yet achieved this recognition.
membershipBasis: Voluntary, values-aligned, opt-in; population scale is explicitly part of the concept (on the order of 1M+ aligned members cited for legitimacy at scale).
fundingTreasury: Crowdfunded territory acquisition; funding mechanisms vary by project (venture capital, membership fees, token treasuries).
representativeExamples: Praxis (territory-seeking, $525M+ raised); Prospera (Honduras ZEDE charter city); Liberland (7 km² territorial claim + Layer-1 governance).
differentiationNote: Unlike a DAO, a Network State explicitly works toward sovereign diplomatic recognition and physical (if non-contiguous) territory — its defining goal. Unlike a Network Nation, which deliberately does not seek territory, a Network State's whole trajectory is territorial: it is the one type here that aims to end up looking like a nation-state.

relations.note: A Network State is explicitly working toward sovereign diplomatic recognition from existing governments.

references.note: The Network State — "The Network State in One Sentence": primary source (Balaji Srinivasan's own site).
The Network State — "On Network States": extended definition, source for the exit-based-governance framing.

Vitalik Buterin — "An Approach to Network State Node Zero" [networkstates essay]: accepts the core network-state premise but argues founder centralization is dangerous at scale and proposes democratic safeguards (soulbound citizen identity over coin voting, exit-to-community, host-community representation) rather than a rival organizational category with its own examples — folded into this row as a critical perspective rather than given a separate table row for that reason.

Collective Intelligence Project — "We need network societies, not network states" (Divya Siddarth, Glen Weyl and Anne-Marie Slaughter): a critique of the network-state model that also summarizes Srinivasan's lifecycle (online community, network union, network archipelago, recognized network state). Source for the lifecycle summary and for the "network society" counter-framing, which is folded into this row instead of getting its own row because it argues against this type rather than describing a separate organizational form.

name: Network Nation
primaryDefinition: 'A digitally-native community that exercises functional sovereignty without exclusive territorial claims' — organizes around shared values and digital governance infrastructure rather than birth-determined citizenship.[c] An active alliance organizes under this term, not just a research framing — a real cooperative alliance of builders, researchers, organizations, and activists, with named members and an active monthly-call cadence, not merely an academic concept.[a][b] The same family of ideas goes by other names: Primavera De Filippi's broader term "CoordiNations" (as Michel Bauwens describes it),[d] and Igor Calzada's "Algorithmic Nations", which a 2024 comparative paper treats as a third paradigm alongside Network States and De Filippi's Network Sovereignties — centred on how stateless, indigenous and diaspora communities can attain self-determination through data sovereignty.[e]
shortDescription: A digitally native community that exercises functional sovereignty without exclusive territorial claims.
governanceModel: Blockchain-based governance tooling: soulbound tokens / Proof-of-Humanity for portable identity, DAOs for treasury management, conviction voting / quadratic funding / participatory budgeting / futarchy for decisions.[c] The alliance describes its governance as polycentric — multiple nested, overlapping, autonomous governance bodies that coexist and coordinate — with legitimacy drawn from active participation, mutual accountability and the renegotiation of shared rules rather than a central mandate.[a]
legalTerritorialStatus: Explicitly does NOT require territory (the key distinction from a Network State) — functions as a supplement to, not a replacement for, nation-states. No existing international legal category recognizes non-territorial polities of this kind.[c] The alliance's stated aim is "functional sovereignty" — the capacity to govern essential domains of community life with a high degree of autonomy, grounded in the ability to set rules and manage resources rather than in territory — working alongside nation-states instead of replacing them.[a]
membershipBasis: Chosen identity, not birthright; portable across communities; members can hold simultaneous memberships in multiple network nations (unlike exclusive nation-state citizenship).[c]
fundingTreasury: Collective crowdfunding and pooled member contributions (e.g. CityDAO's $8M+ land purchase); tokenized DAO treasury management for some examples — funding mechanisms vary by project, no single unified model.[c]
representativeExamples: CityDAO (5,000+ members, 40 acres in Wyoming); Zuzalu (2-month pop-up city, Montenegro 2023); Edge City (professionalized pop-up village format); Liberland (7 km² territorial claim + Layer-1 governance).[c]
differentiationNote: Unlike a Network State, a Network Nation explicitly does not require or seek territory — it functions as a supplement to existing nation-states, not a competitor to them. Unlike a DAO's token-based voting, it leans on portable identity tooling (soulbound tokens, Proof-of-Humanity) and mechanism-design tools like quadratic funding for decision-making, and its alliance describes governance as polycentric rather than centrally mandated.

relatedTechnology.capability: Portable identity and proof of personhood
relatedTechnology.note: Its governance model relies on portable identity such as soulbound tokens and Proof-of-Humanity; the listed projects are examples of proof-of-personhood and identity tooling in the Navigator.
Its governance tooling is blockchain-based, with DAOs used for treasury management; Ethereum and Solana are listed as examples of platforms that run such contracts.

relatedMechanisms.note: Its governance tooling names quadratic funding among the mechanisms used for decisions and funding.

references.note: Network Nations Alliance — "What is a Network Nation?" essay: the alliance's own primary framing source, confirming it operates as a real cooperative alliance of builders, researchers, organizations, and activists — not just a research framing. Includes named members, a public monthly-call calendar, and a direct comparison table contrasting Network Nations (bottom-up, commons-logic, cooperative) against Network States (top-down, investor-driven, exit-based).

Network Nations Alliance — The Garden: the alliance's community knowledge-graph/gathering hub (concepts, constitution, reading list, organizations, events) — corroborates [a]'s active-alliance evidence with its own ongoing-activity structure.

Gitcoin Research — "Network Nations: Building Sovereignty Without Land": primary source for the network-nation definition, governance-model framing (soulbound tokens/Proof of Humanity, DAO treasury management, conviction voting/quadratic funding/futarchy), and the representative examples (CityDAO, Zuzalu, Edge City, Liberland).

Michel Bauwens — "The Age of Trans-Local Self-Organized CoordiNations" (Substack, 29 April 2024): the visible preview credits "CoordiNations" as a more generic concept developed by Primavera De Filippi, discussed alongside network nations and network states. The essay body is paywalled and was not read for this entry; only that attribution is relied on.

Future Internet 2024, 16(10), 361 — "Decentralized Web3 Reshaping Internet Governance: Towards the Emergence of New Forms of Nation-Statehood?": compares three paradigms — Network States (Srinivasan), Network Sovereignties (De Filippi) and Algorithmic Nations (Calzada, communities such as indigenous and stateless groups and e-diasporas attaining self-determination through data sovereignty). Source for the Algorithmic Nations description and for treating it as a related framing folded into this row, not a separate row.

name: NAO (Networked Adaptive Organism)
primaryDefinition: DAOs whose populations are Trust Networks, with an innate capacity for 'extreme decisioning' beyond ordinary coordination.[a] The NAO, stewarded by Allelo, is the only real-world instance known to be operating today — more NAOs may emerge as the concept develops.[b]
shortDescription: A DAO whose population is a trust network, with a capacity for 'extreme decisioning' beyond ordinary coordination.
governanceModel: Web-of-trust identity and liquid-democracy-style delegation, rather than token voting.[a] The NAO, stewarded by Allelo, coordinates via Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs), pooled resources, and incentive-alignment mechanisms across startups, investors, and communities.[b][d] Its origin source describes allocating collective value "as a fractal commons",[a] and none of the sources reviewed describes any body holding control over the participating SPVs and communities, which is why it is scored fully decentralized.[d]
legalTerritorialStatus: No inherent territorial ambition — envisioned as a self-owning, self-governing social graph organized as a platform cooperative rather than a single legal entity.[a] In practice, The NAO is stewarded by Allelo, a Netherlands-registered legal entity (jurisdiction not independently confirmed this pass), which uses SPVs as conventional legal wrappers for participating ventures and communities rather than one overarching entity.[b][d] Platform cooperatives — cooperatives that sell through a website, app or protocol with democratic decision-making and shared ownership by workers and users[e] — are a broader, older cooperative form that this table does not list separately; the NAO's own source describes it as organized as one.[a][f]
membershipBasis: Membership and trust are established via web-of-trust identity rather than token-holding[a] — GreenCheck's three-friend authentication is one independent example of this approach.[c] The NAO's membership, per Allelo's framing, spans purpose-driven communities, regenerative ventures, and patient-capital investors opting into a shared value-creation network.[b][d]
fundingTreasury: Envisioned as capturing collective value at scale and allocating it emergently, 'as a fractal commons' — no specific treasury mechanism beyond that.[a] The NAO, via Allelo, pools patient capital using SPVs and shared resource pools, oriented toward regenerative, civilisational-scale value creation.[b][d]
representativeExamples: The NAO — the only operating NAO known to exist, stewarded by Allelo (a Netherlands-registered legal entity per direct sourcing, not independently confirmed this pass; not itself a NAO); more NAOs may emerge as the concept develops.[a][b]
differentiationNote: Unlike the other types, a NAO's own primary source frames it explicitly as a subtype of DAO ('DAOs whose populations are Trust Networks'), not a peer category — it adds a web-of-trust population model and liquid-democracy-style decision-making on top of DAO infrastructure, rather than rejecting DAO tooling the way a Network State or Network Nation's territorial/identity focus does.

relatedTechnology.note: A NAO is defined by a population that forms a trust network, which needs identity built on verifiable trust between people; GreenCheck comes from the same NooNAO lineage, and BrightID and Verifiable Relationship Credentials are listed as further examples.

relations.note: Its own primary source frames the NAO as 'DAOs whose populations are Trust Networks'.

references.note: nao.is (NooNAO) — "Toward Wise Emergent Coordination for a Less Bad Future": PRIMARY source — the origin of the NAO term, created by one of the NAO's founders. Site returns a bare JS-SPA shell to automated fetch — full homepage text sourced directly and quoted verbatim in this table. The site is largely inactive today and does not reflect a currently operating organization — useful for explaining the underlying concept, not as a source of current real-world examples.

Allelo's own site (a password-gated members-only landing page as of 2026-08-24) — the entry screen, visible without the passphrase, carries this tagline: "NAO (Network Adaptive Organism) is a gamified societal infrastructure — a living network where purpose-driven communities, regenerative ventures, and patient capital converge to co-create shared value at civilisational scale." Uses a close variant of nao.is's term ("Network Adaptive Organism" vs. nao.is's "Networked Adaptive Organisms"). The site itself does not state jurisdiction, founder, or SPV/pooled-resources mechanics — see reference [d] for independent corroboration of the SPV/pooled-resources framing specifically (jurisdiction and founder remain unconfirmed by any source reviewed).

protocols.json (this site's own data, id: greencheck): independent internal corroboration — this project's own Matrix data (GreenCheck identity protocol, built by NooNAO/nao.is) separately uses "Networked Adaptive Organisms" and frames them as "trust-network-based DAOs", matching nao.is's own wording exactly. GreenCheck is a separate, legitimate Matrix entry as an identity protocol, not itself a NAO instance.

profiles.eco business profile for Allelo (registered .eco-domain entity, activated 2025-02-19; listed as a "Business", no jurisdiction or founder disclosed) — independently corroborates the SPV/pooled-resources/shared-governance framing nearly verbatim: "Allelo is guiding startups and investors towards cooperative ecosystems where they, along with service providers and communities, collaborate using tools such as Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs), pooled resources, and shared governance frameworks." Confirms Allelo stewards The NAO; does not confirm jurisdiction (Netherlands) or founder — neither is independently confirmed via any public source reviewed for this entry.

Platform Cooperativism Consortium (platform.coop): describes platform co-ops as businesses that sell goods or services mainly through a website, app or protocol, with democratic decision-making and shared ownership by workers and users. Source for what a platform cooperative is; folded into the NAO row, not given its own row, because it is a general cooperative form rather than a distinct network-scale governance model.

International Co-operative Alliance — "Cooperative identity, values & principles": defines a cooperative as an autonomous association of persons united voluntarily to meet common economic, social and cultural needs through a jointly owned and democratically controlled enterprise (statement adopted 1995). Source for the general definition of a cooperative.

name: cDPO (Commons-Oriented Decentralised Programmed Organisation)
primaryDefinition: A framework to bootstrap, develop, and sustain commons projects — the commons-oriented counterpart to a DAO. Rather than offering the commons good itself as the thing of value, a cDPO offers peer-participants shared stakes in the organisation that creates it: "much like offering people to join in a fishing trip instead of offering the fishes already caught."[a][b]
shortDescription: A framework for bootstrapping and sustaining commons projects by offering participants shared stakes in the organization behind them.
governanceModel: Peer-participants receive an "equity-like currency" — tokens issued as recognition of the value they generate through interaction with/within the organisation, explicitly not payment for services and not company stock ("sovereign notions of value produced in the interaction"). Each token carries two functions: governance value within the project, and liquidity through third-party value recognition.[a][b]
legalTerritorialStatus: No inherent territorial ambition. Documented as a design pattern for structuring an organisation, not tied to any specific legal wrapper — the primary source describes the bootstrapping and token-issuance process in economic rather than jurisdictional terms, and no deployed instance exists yet to establish an actual legal precedent.[a][b]
membershipBasis: Peer-participants who generate value through interaction with the organisation, recognised via token issuance along one of two paths: "pre-issuance" (tokens sold upfront to bootstrap the organisation, e.g. to acquire a shared asset or fund initial development) or "emerging valuation" (tokens issued over time as contributions happen, no upfront asset needed).[a][b]
fundingTreasury: Value recognition requires a third party and is drawn from three named sources: donations, grants, and pledges into a shared pool (cited as significant for retrospective valuation by public institutions); fiat from third-party commercial use or remixing of the commons output (e.g. via a peer production licence); and cross-organisation value recognition, where one project’s token is accepted in exchange for another project’s value offer — illustrated with a worked example of a city accepting a cDPO’s tokens as public transit fare.[a][b]
representativeExamples: No confirmed operating instance found as of 2026-09-04. The concept is documented by its originators as a design pattern and bootstrapping process, not (yet) observed deployed by any named organisation — unlike this table’s other rows, no real-world cDPO has been independently identified.[a][b]
differentiationNote: Unlike a DAO, a cDPO is a design pattern for structuring an organisation rather than a deployed technology stack, and its tokens are explicitly not payment or company stock but an equity-like currency recognising contribution, carrying both governance value and liquidity. Unlike a NAO or a DisCO, no operating instance has been identified, and unlike a Network State or Network Nation it makes no territorial or sovereignty claim at all.

relatedMechanisms.note: The cDPO concept comes from the Economic Space Agency team, whose protocol grammar for plural economic instruments is the mechanism listed here.

references.note: P2P Foundation Wiki — "Commons-Oriented Decentralised Programmed Organisations": the live site returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; read via a full local mirror of the wiki instead (see this story’s Context section). The page’s entire substantive content is itself a direct quote of reference [b] — source for the core definition, the "equity-like currency" mechanism, the pre-issuance/emerging-valuation distinction, and the three liquidity sources.

ECSA Team (Economic Space Agency) — "Programmed Decentralised Commons Production," Medium, 2017: ultimate primary source: the wiki page at [a] is a direct quote of this article. Originates the cDPO concept, the fishing-trip framing, the two token functions (governance + liquidity), and the full bootstrapping-process sequence (liquidity → DPO design → pre-sale/escrow → token issuance → stakeholder status → liquidate-or-hold).

name: DisCO (Distributed Cooperative Organization)
primaryDefinition: A cooperative governance and economic model that tracks pro-bono commons work, paid ("livelihood") work and care work as three separate value streams — presented by its authors as a cooperative, commons-oriented, feminist-economics alternative to Decentralized Autonomous Organizations.[a][b][c]
shortDescription: A cooperative model that tracks pro-bono commons work, paid work, and care work as three separate value streams.
governanceModel: The default decision protocol is virtually identical to a traditional co-op's one-member-one-vote, with members' shares able to influence decisions in critical situations such as a blocked proposal; decisions and control are otherwise shared on the basis of contributions and peer review.[c] Its authors foreground association over autonomy and federation over scale.[d]
legalTerritorialStatus: No territorial ambition. A model a collective adopts rather than a legal form: its pilot, Guerrilla Translation (part of the Guerrilla Media Collective), is described as an Open Cooperative.[d] No DisCO-specific legal wrapper was documented in the sources reviewed.
membershipBasis: Worker-members who each hold shares across the three work streams. Participation is opt-in and equipotential: anyone who joins as a member has their work valued and is expected to take part in decisions.[c]
fundingTreasury: Value created by the collective's productive work (for Guerrilla Translation: written and simultaneous translation, copyediting and subtitling) is converted to money through a market-facing agency, pooled, and paid out monthly according to each member's shares across the three streams.[c]
representativeExamples: Guerrilla Translation / the Guerrilla Media Collective — the archetype the model was drawn from.[d] No other operating DisCO was verified for this entry.
differentiationNote: Unlike a DAO — which its authors position it against as individualistic and techno-deterministic — a DisCO is organized around a cooperative's membership and three tracked work streams (pro-bono commons work, paid work, care work) rather than around code-enforced rules, though its authors see a role for distributed-ledger tools in its value accounting. Unlike a cDPO, whose defining feature is a tokenized, equity-like stake, a DisCO's documented core is share-based accounting of work inside a cooperative; the similar acronyms are a coincidence of naming, not a lineage.

references.note: DisCO.coop: describes DisCO as an approach for organizations that want to create and share value in ways that are cooperative, commons-oriented and rooted in feminist economics. Primary source for the self-description.

If I Only Had a Heart: A DisCO Manifesto (2019): describes DisCOs as a P2P/Commons, cooperative and feminist-economic alternative to DAOs, and the Guerrilla Translation / Guerrilla Media Collective origin of the model. Primary source for the DAO-contrast framing.

P2P Foundation Wiki — "Distributed Cooperative Organization": quotes the Guerrilla Media Collective's DisCO Governance Model v3.0 and Guerrilla Translation's own description (three work streams, shares, monthly payout, one-member-one-vote default, opt-in equipotential membership). Read via a local mirror of the wiki; the Guerrilla Media Collective wiki that originates these quotes did not resolve when checked.

P2P Foundation Wiki — "Distributed Cooperative Organizations": quotes Morshed Mannan's summary of the DisCO Manifesto (association over autonomy, federation over scale; the Guerrilla Media Collective as archetype) and identifies Guerrilla Translation as an Open Cooperative and DisCO pilot. Read via a local mirror of the wiki.

name: Nation-State
primaryDefinition: A sovereign territorial state whose population is, or is treated as, a single nation — the default baseline for territorial governance that every other type in this table defines itself against. International law's classic test says a state should have a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states.[a]
shortDescription: A sovereign territorial state whose population is, or is treated as, a single nation; the default baseline for territorial governance.
governanceModel: A government exercising authority over its territory and population, in forms that vary widely (republics, monarchies, federations, one-party states), so no single decision mechanism defines the type. A state's political existence does not depend on other states recognizing it.[a]
legalTerritorialStatus: The only type here with sovereign legal personality in international law and recognized jurisdiction over a defined territory (one of the four qualifications above).[a] States admitted to the United Nations are listed on its member-state roll.[b]
membershipBasis: Citizenship, typically by birth (descent or birthplace) or by naturalization; it is not chosen the way membership in the other types is, and whether multiple citizenships are allowed depends on each state's own law.
fundingTreasury: Taxation, backed by the state's monopoly on legitimate coercion, supplemented by borrowing and, for states that issue their own currency, monetary issuance.
representativeExamples: Every member state of the United Nations claims this form; how closely a single national identity coincides with the state varies widely.[b]
differentiationNote: Unlike every other type here, a nation-state is the baseline the rest define themselves against: it holds recognized sovereignty over a defined territory and a permanent population, membership is by citizenship rather than choice, and it is funded by taxation. A Network State aims to become one, a Network Nation deliberately works alongside one, and a DAO, NAO, cDPO or DisCO makes no such claim.

relatedMechanisms.note: A state that issues its own currency funds itself partly through monetary issuance, which is the mechanism described as fiat sovereign currency.

relations.note: A corporation is a legal person created under, and subject to, the law of the jurisdiction where it is incorporated.
A nonprofit is a legal person created under, and subject to, the law of its jurisdiction.

references.note: Organization of American States — Convention on Rights and Duties of States (1933): Article 1 lists the four qualifications of a state (permanent population, defined territory, government, capacity to enter into relations with other states); Article 3 states that a state's political existence is independent of recognition by other states. The page body is scanned images, so the articles were read from the scan.
United Nations — Member States: the roll of states admitted to the UN, each with a date of admission.

name: For-Profit Corporation
primaryDefinition: A legally incorporated company owned by shareholders and run to generate profit for them — the default baseline for hierarchical, equity-owned organization. Under Delaware's General Corporation Law, one concrete statute, a corporation may be incorporated to conduct or promote any lawful business or purposes.[a]
shortDescription: A legally incorporated company owned by shareholders and run for their profit; the default baseline for equity-owned organization.
governanceModel: The business and affairs of the corporation are managed by or under the direction of a board of directors, which oversees the executives who run day-to-day operations.[b] Shareholders elect the directors and vote on certain major matters in proportion to the shares they hold.
legalTerritorialStatus: A legal person created under, and subject to, the law of the jurisdiction where it is incorporated; it makes no territorial claim and has no sovereignty of its own.[a]
membershipBasis: Employment for workers and share ownership for owners; customers and the public are not members. Ownership is typically transferable — shares can be bought and sold.
fundingTreasury: Equity (selling shares), debt, and revenue from selling goods or services; profits are retained or distributed to shareholders.
representativeExamples: Ubiquitous; listed as a baseline for comparison, not as a catalog of companies.
differentiationNote: Unlike a DAO, NAO, cDPO or DisCO, a for-profit corporation's governance rests on a board answerable to shareholders, and its purpose is profit for them. It is the baseline for hierarchical, equity-owned organization — what the commons- and cooperative-oriented types in this table position themselves against. Unlike a nonprofit, residual profit goes to its owners.

references.note: Delaware Code, Title 8, Chapter 1 (General Corporation Law), Subchapter I — Formation: §101(b) allows a corporation to be incorporated to conduct or promote any lawful business or purposes; §102(a)(3) lets the certificate state that purpose generally. Used as one concrete statute, not as a claim that Delaware law is universal.

Delaware Code, Title 8, Chapter 1, Subchapter IV — Directors and Officers: §141(a) provides that the business and affairs of a corporation are managed by or under the direction of a board of directors, subject to any provision in the chapter or the certificate of incorporation.

name: Nonprofit Organization
primaryDefinition: A mission-driven organization with formal legal personhood but no owners entitled to its profits — the default baseline for non-equity organization. In US federal tax law, a 501(c)(3) organization must be organized and operated exclusively for exempt purposes, and none of its earnings may inure to any private shareholder or individual.[a]
shortDescription: A mission-driven organization with legal personhood and no owners entitled to its profits; the default baseline for non-equity organization.
governanceModel: Typically a board of directors or trustees accountable to the mission rather than to owners; whether members vote, and whether the board is elected or self-perpetuating, depends on the organization's bylaws and the law of its jurisdiction.
legalTerritorialStatus: A legal person created under, and subject to, the law of its jurisdiction; it makes no territorial claim. In the US, tax-exempt status adds conditions — a 501(c)(3) may not attempt to influence legislation as a substantial part of its activities and may not take part in political-campaign activity.[a]
membershipBasis: No ownership stake: staff are employed, and volunteers and donors take part out of agreement with the mission; membership nonprofits admit members under their bylaws.
fundingTreasury: Donations, grants, membership dues and earned revenue; any surplus is reinvested in the mission rather than distributed. In the US, 501(c)(3) organizations can receive tax-deductible contributions.[a]
representativeExamples: Ubiquitous; listed as a baseline for comparison, not as a catalog of organizations.
differentiationNote: Unlike a corporation, a nonprofit has no owners entitled to its profits — in US tax law, none of a 501(c)(3)'s earnings may go to a private shareholder or individual.[a] Unlike a DAO, it has formal legal personhood and usually a board accountable to its mission rather than on-chain voting. It is the baseline for mission-driven, non-equity organization.

references.note: IRS — Exemption requirements, 501(c)(3) organizations (page reviewed or updated 28 June 2026): organizational and operational tests, the prohibition on private inurement, limits on lobbying and political-campaign activity, and eligibility for tax-deductible contributions. A US-law illustration of the form, not a claim that the rules are universal.

name: GAN (Global Action Network)
primaryDefinition: A multi-stakeholder network that spans geographical, institutional and sectoral boundaries — involving business, government and the social sector — to work on global problems no single sector resolves, in Steve Waddell's framework.[a]
shortDescription: A multi-stakeholder network across geographic, institutional, and sectoral lines, working on global problems no single sector can solve.
governanceModel: Multi-stakeholder governance that either balances the sectors or deliberately reserves co-ownership to chosen groups. Boards are usually elected by the co-owners, with "seats" for specific stakeholder groups to ensure voice for a constituency, and GANs "adopt traditions from government and NGOs to plan, set policy, and vote".[c] Waddell separates participants from co-owners (the members with decision rights) and describes three structures: participation becomes co-ownership, as at the Forest Stewardship Council, where environmental, social and economic chambers hold equal voting weight in a General Assembly that elects the board;[b][c] participation is separated from co-ownership, as at the Principles for Responsible Investment (asset owners in charge, the other signatory categories participants only) and the Global Compact (the UN is owner); and ownership is closed to sponsors, as at the Global Water Partnership.[c] The Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, which calls itself a multi-stakeholder initiative, fixes each sector's share of the vote (25% for growers, 12.5% for each of six other sectors).[d] How a GAN is governed changes as it develops.[c]
legalTerritorialStatus: No territorial claim. Participants span the governmental, nonprofit and private sectors, so the form is defined by its multi-sector membership rather than by a single legal status or jurisdiction.[a] Waddell notes that GANs lack "an appropriate legal form": the network itself is "a square peg in a round hole", the Secretariat "almost always" incorporates as an NGO, and some, such as the Global Water Partnership, obtain intergovernmental-organization status.[c]
membershipBasis: Participants from each sector who join around a shared issue. Membership is "usually ... a written commitment to a set of goals or principles", and the right to vote (co-ownership) is usually tied to signing on to those principles.[c] GANs are inter-organizational networks where individuals mostly have no role, with exceptions;[c] the FSC, for example, has over 1,300 individual and organizational members grouped into three chambers.[b] A network may exclude stakeholders whose goals conflict with its own: the Tobacco-Free Initiative bars tobacco companies from participating.[c]
fundingTreasury: No single treasury model is documented in the sources reviewed for this entry; funding varies by network.[a] Some networks require dues, often limited to or higher for companies; the Fair Labor Association, for example, uses a sliding scale with a US$5,000 minimum.[c]
representativeExamples: Forest Stewardship Council (which a 2011 review credits with certifying about 300 million acres of forest); the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria; the Principles for Responsible Investment.[a] Waddell also treats Transparency International, the Global Compact and the Global Reporting Initiative as GANs.[c] OpenHaven also includes the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, which describes itself as a multi-stakeholder initiative; it is not named in the sources reviewed for Waddell's list.[d]
differentiationNote: Unlike a single nonprofit or corporation, a GAN is a network of participants from the governmental, nonprofit and private sectors, with governance that either balances the sectors (the Forest Stewardship Council's equal-weight chambers) or reserves co-ownership to one group while the others take part (the PRI's asset owners).[b][c] Unlike a Network Nation or a DisCO, it is organized around a shared issue rather than a shared identity or way of life, and unlike a DAO it is not defined by on-chain governance. The sources reviewed document commitment to a network's principles as the basis of membership; they do not document admission by an identity or "resonance" filter, or by vouching from existing members.[c]

references.note: Stanford Social Innovation Review — review (Fall 2011, Patrick McNamara) of Steve Waddell, Global Action Networks: Creating Our Future Together (Palgrave Macmillan, 2011): defines GANs as multi-stakeholder networks spanning geographical, institutional and sectoral boundaries to effect systemic change, involving business, government and the social sector; lists the Global Fund, FSC and the Principles for Responsible Investment as examples. Cited for the book's framework.

Forest Stewardship Council — Governance (page read 21 November 2026): the General Assembly (all members, meeting every three years) is the highest decision-making body; members join one of three chambers (environmental, social, economic) of equal voting weight (33.3% each), each split equally between North and South sub-chambers, with individual members holding 10% and organizational members 90% within each sub-chamber; the Assembly elects the Board; over 1,300 individual and organizational members.

Steve Waddell, Global Action Networks: Creating Our Future Together (Palgrave Macmillan, 2011), Chapter 6, "Formalizing the connections" (pp. 123-141): distinguishes participants from co-owners (Table 6.1), describes structures that turn participation into co-ownership, separate the two, or close ownership to sponsors, and covers membership as commitment to principles, boards with constituency seats, and legal structure. Cited for how GANs are governed and organized.

Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO), Statutes 2024 (endorsed by its General Assembly on 13 November 2024) and governance page (https://rspo.org/about/governance/): the Statutes fix each membership sector's voting weight (growers 25%, six other sectors 12.5% each) and establish RSPO as an association under Swiss law; the governance page describes it as "a global, multi-stakeholder initiative". Cited for RSPO's sector vote shares.

name: Open-Process Consensus Body
primaryDefinition: A body whose authority rests on a documented, open process of discussion aimed at consensus, with a defined path for objections, rather than on ownership, a board's orders or sector chambers. No party owns what it produces. Participation is open to any interested person (the IETF) or to member organizations that join and pay (W3C), and an incorporated body carries the administration and the money. The IETF and W3C, which use the process to write open technical standards, are the examples.[a][d][e]
shortDescription: A body whose authority rests on an open, documented process of discussion toward consensus, with no owner of its output.
governanceModel: Decisions come from open discussion aimed at consensus, not from owners or sector chambers. In the IETF a working group chair judges "rough consensus", which is not a vote,[b] and the participating individual, not the organization, is the fundamental unit.[a] In W3C, "consensus is a core value"; objections go through a Formal Objection process that can end in a W3C Council, Team decisions derive from the CEO's authority, and a Board of Directors oversees the Team and the budget.[e]
legalTerritorialStatus: No territorial claim. The legal form varies by body. The IETF community has no legal entity of its own: its administration sits in the IETF LLC, a disregarded limited liability company of the Internet Society.[c] W3C is itself an international public-interest non-profit organization.[d]
membershipBasis: Participation grounded in a shared commitment to the work. IETF participants "come to the IETF because they want to do work that furthers the IETF's mission", and "any interested person can participate".[a] W3C membership is by organization, with fees that vary by revenue, type and location of headquarters; the public also takes part.[d][f]
fundingTreasury: Varies by body. The IETF LLC's income comes from Internet Society support, IETF meeting revenues, sponsorships and donations, and it files an annual IRS Form 990.[c] W3C's revenues "come primarily from Membership dues", with some grants.[d]
representativeExamples: Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF); World Wide Web Consortium (W3C).[a][d]
differentiationNote: Unlike a GAN, which brings sectors together around a shared issue and gives each a chamber, authority here rests on an open process, and people or paying members take part in their own right, not as a sector's representatives. Unlike a nonprofit, decisions come from consensus among participants, not from a board's hierarchy, even though a board exists for administration. Unlike bodies such as ISO, whose deliberations are open only to formal members who are delegates of national standards bodies, or the ITU, governed by treaty among national bodies, the process itself is open.[g]

references.note: RFC 3935, A Mission Statement for the IETF (October 2004): states the open-process principle ("any interested person can participate"), that individuals are the fundamental unit, that participants are a volunteer core, and the "rough consensus and running code" principle. Cited for participation and decision-making.
RFC 7282, On Consensus and Humming in the IETF (June 2014): explains that rough consensus is not a vote and that a working group chair can declare it. Cited for the decision rule.

RFC 8711, Structure of the IETF Administrative Support Activity, Version 2.0 (February 2020): defines the IETF LLC as a disregarded limited liability company of the Internet Society and lists its income sources (Internet Society support, meeting revenues, sponsorships, donations). Cited for legal form and funding.

W3C, About (page read 21 November 2026): describes W3C as an international public-interest non-profit organization funded primarily by Membership dues, whose decisions are taken by consensus. Cited for W3C's legal form, funding and decision rule.

W3C Process Document (18 August 2025): states that consensus is a core value, sets the Formal Objection and W3C Council path, and places Team decisions under the CEO's authority and the Board of Directors' oversight. Cited for W3C's decision process.
W3C, Membership (page read 21 November 2026): states that Membership fees vary with annual revenue, type and headquarters location. Cited for how Members pay.

Kaliya Young and Day Davis Waterbury, Exploring the Remarkable Regenerative Patterns and Practices of the Internet Engineering Task Force (v1.0, November 2024; funded by Ethereum Foundation's Summer of Protocols): contrasts the IETF with the ISO, ITU and IEEE and describes its individual participation and structure. Cited for the comparison with closed standards bodies.

name: Community of Contributors
primaryDefinition: A community that maintains a shared specification or codebase in public repositories without a legal entity of its own. A list of maintainers with commit rights decides what is merged, by review and rough agreement, anyone can propose a change or fork the work, and no one can force software to adopt the result.[a][b][c]
shortDescription: People who maintain a shared specification or codebase in public, with no legal entity; maintainers decide what merges.
governanceModel: Maintainer-gated open contribution. Anyone can propose a change in the open; the maintainers decide what merges. Cashu's specification repository requires "a minimum of two approving reviews from core Cashu maintainers and contributors" and at least two implementation pull requests across different projects before a change merges.[b] Nostr's repository merges a proposal "once most people reasonably agree", its owner can revoke maintainers' membership, and if that is "perceived as bad or evil the community must react", and the index can fork.[a] "Nothing forces any software to implement any NIP."[a] Valueflows works through issues and pull requests.[c]
legalTerritorialStatus: No territorial claim, and no legal entity: the community is the people who maintain the work. The governing documents read for this entry name none; the Valueflows domain name is held by two individuals.[c]
membershipBasis: Participation by contribution. Anyone can raise an issue, fork a repository or send a pull request.[c] Maintainers are those with commit access, which the existing maintainers or the repository owner grant, and Valueflows' organization on its code host is by invitation.[a][c]
fundingTreasury: No treasury is documented in the governing documents. Work is funded by grants to contributors: OpenSats says its Nostr Fund "pays grants to relay operators, client developers, library maintainers, designers, and protocol-level" contributors, and lists "Cashu by Cashu Contributors" among the projects its General Fund supports.[d][e] Valueflows' funding is not stated in the sources read.
representativeExamples: Cashu (the NUTs specification and its reference libraries); Nostr (the NIPs repository); Valueflows (a vocabulary for economic coordination).[a][b][c]
differentiationNote: Unlike a DisCO, it has no cooperative structure, shared treasury or shared accounting. Unlike a DAO, nothing is decided by token. Unlike an open-process consensus body such as the IETF, it has no incorporated body or appeal path: its process is a repository's contribution guide. Unlike a nonprofit, there is no board.

references.note: Nostr NIPs repository, README (read 21 November 2026): describes how NIPs emerge, who has commit access, that the repository owner can revoke membership, that the index can fork, and that nothing forces any software to implement a NIP. Cited for governance.

Cashu NUTs repository, Contributing guide (read 21 November 2026): requires two approving reviews from core maintainers and contributors and two implementation pull requests across different projects before a specification change merges. Cited for the decision rule.

Valueflows repository, README (read 21 November 2026): invites participation through issues, forks and pull requests, says joining the Valueflows organization requires an invitation, and states who holds the domain. Cited for participation and structure.

OpenSats, The Nostr Fund (read 21 November 2026): says the fund pays grants to relay operators, client developers, library maintainers, designers and protocol-level contributors. Cited for how Nostr work is funded.
OpenSats, Projects (read 21 November 2026): lists "Cashu by Cashu Contributors" among the projects its General Fund supports. Cited for how Cashu work is funded.

name: Stakeholder-Governed Corporation
primaryDefinition: A for-profit corporation whose charter commits it to a public benefit and obliges its directors to balance the owners' financial interests with those of the people and communities the company affects. The commitment comes from a statute (the benefit corporation and public benefit corporation laws of many US states; in the UK, the community interest company) or from a charter amendment that a private certifier such as B Lab requires.[a][b][c]
shortDescription: A for-profit company whose charter writes a public benefit into its purpose and obliges directors to balance several interests, not only profit.
governanceModel: Directors keep ordinary corporate control but carry a duty written into the charter. In Delaware, a public benefit corporation "shall be managed in a manner that balances the stockholders' pecuniary interests, the best interests of those materially affected by the corporation's conduct, and the public benefit or public benefits identified in its certificate of incorporation".[a] Under the model legislation B Lab describes, directors must consider the impact of their decisions on all stakeholders and the company reports publicly on how it did; Delaware's version asks for a report to shareholders every two years.[b]
legalTerritorialStatus: No territorial claim. A registered company. A benefit corporation is "a legal status administered by your Secretary of State or similar role in each state, province, or country", a layer on top of the traditional corporate status; the term differs between jurisdictions, and some US states use "public benefit corporation" for entities such as nonprofits.[b] The UK community interest company is "a new type of company" created by the Companies (Audit, Investigations and Community Enterprise) Act 2004, whose activities must pass a community interest test.[c]
membershipBasis: Membership is shareholding, as in any corporation. The duty to consider workers, suppliers, the environment and other stakeholders binds the directors; it does not make those stakeholders members.[b]
fundingTreasury: Equity investment and profit, as in any company. The charter does not remove the owners' claim on surplus; it adds a duty to balance it against the public benefit.[a]
representativeExamples: Bluesky Social, PBC, which provides the Bluesky application on the AT Protocol.[d] Certified B Corps, which B Lab describes as for-profit legal entities.[b]
differentiationNote: Unlike a conventional for-profit corporation, whose directors answer to profit, its charter adds a public benefit and a duty to balance interests. Unlike a nonprofit, it keeps equity and pays profit to owners. Unlike a steward-owned company, control still follows shareholding.

references.note: Delaware Code, Title 8, Chapter 1, Subchapter XV (Public Benefit Corporations), s. 362: defines a public benefit corporation as a for-profit corporation managed to balance the stockholders' pecuniary interests, the interests of those materially affected and the public benefit stated in its certificate of incorporation. Cited for the form's legal definition and duty.

B Lab, "Benefit Corporation vs. B Corp" (page read 21 November 2026): separates the benefit corporation (a legal status layered on the corporate status and administered by the state) from B Corp certification (a private certification of for-profit legal entities that requires a legal commitment to stakeholder governance), and compares the model legislation with Delaware's. Cited for the statute-versus-certification distinction.
Companies (Audit, Investigations and Community Enterprise) Act 2004, Part 2 (UK), ss. 26 and 35: creates the community interest company and its community interest test. Cited for the UK variant.
Bluesky Social, PBC, Terms of Service (14 August 2025): states that Bluesky is provided by Bluesky Social, PBC and runs on the AT Protocol. Cited as an adopter.

name: Cooperative
primaryDefinition: "An autonomous association of persons united voluntarily to meet their common economic, social and cultural needs and aspirations through a jointly-owned and democratically-controlled enterprise", in the statement of identity of the International Cooperative Alliance.[a] The form is set by cooperative statutes (for example the European Cooperative Society, whose principal object is "the satisfaction of its members' needs and/or the development of their economic and/or social activities")[b] and by seven principles the Alliance maintains.[a]
shortDescription: An enterprise owned and democratically controlled by its members, who share its surplus by use and hold part of its capital in common.
governanceModel: "Democratic organisations controlled by their members": in primary cooperatives members have "equal voting rights (one member, one vote)", elected representatives are accountable to the membership, and cooperatives at other levels are also organised democratically.[a] Cooperatives work "together through local, national, regional and international structures".[a]
legalTerritorialStatus: No territorial claim. A registered enterprise under cooperative law; the European Union provides a cross-border form, the European Cooperative Society.[b]
membershipBasis: Voluntary and open: "open to all persons able to use their services and willing to accept the responsibilities of membership".[a] Members are usually also customers, employees or suppliers of the cooperative, or otherwise involved in its activities.[b]
fundingTreasury: Members "contribute equitably to, and democratically control, the capital"; "at least part of that capital is usually the common property of the cooperative"; members "usually receive limited compensation, if any, on capital subscribed". Surpluses go to reserves (at least part of which is indivisible), to "benefiting members in proportion to their transactions with the cooperative" and to other activities the membership approves.[a]
representativeExamples: Stocksy, "an artist-run stock cooperative";[c] MONDRAGON, "the outcome of a cooperative business project launched in 1956".[d]
differentiationNote: Unlike a for-profit corporation, control follows membership, not shares, and capital is partly common property. Unlike a nonprofit, the members own the enterprise and share its surplus by their use of it. Unlike a DisCO, which is a written model that may use a cooperative wrapper, it is a registered legal form with statutory rules.

references.note: International Cooperative Alliance, "Cooperative identity, values & principles" (page read 21 November 2026): the statement on the cooperative identity and the seven principles (voluntary and open membership, democratic member control, member economic participation, cooperation among cooperatives and others). Cited for the definition, the governance and the capital rules.

Council Regulation (EC) No 1435/2003 of 22 July 2003 on the Statute for a European Cooperative Society (SCE), recital 10: the SCE's principal object is the satisfaction of its members' needs, its members are also customers, employees or suppliers, and control is vested equally in members. Cited for a statutory cooperative form.
Stocksy, About Us (page read 21 November 2026): describes Stocksy as an artist-run stock cooperative. Cited as a web-platform cooperative.

MONDRAGON, About us (page read 21 November 2026): describes MONDRAGON as the outcome of a cooperative business project launched in 1956, with values that include intercooperation, grassroots management and democratic organisation. Cited as a large cooperative group.

name: Steward-Owned Company
primaryDefinition: A company guided by two principles. Self-determination: it "cannot become an object of speculation but remains self-determined and independent in the long term", with control kept "in the hands of people who are connected to the company and its mission". Purpose-orientation: "Profits are a means to an end, not an end in themselves."[a] In practice a purpose-bound foundation or trust often holds the controlling shares, as at Proton, where the foundation is "the largest voting shareholder" and "no change of control can occur without the consent of the foundation".[b]
shortDescription: A company whose control is held by people tied to its mission, often through a purpose-bound foundation, so it cannot be sold for speculation.
governanceModel: Voting control and economic benefit are separated: control rests with the stewards (people tied to the company, or a foundation or trust they hold it through), and "the value created within the company cannot be extracted by the company owners".[a] A foundation can hold a veto over a change of control, as at Proton.[b]
legalTerritorialStatus: No territorial claim. A registered company; the model has been implemented in several countries, so the legal vehicle (a foundation, a trust, a golden share) varies and is not a form of its own.[a]
membershipBasis: Control passes to people connected to the company and its mission, not to whoever can buy shares.[a]
fundingTreasury: Equity capital as in any company, but profits "serve the company's mission and development, can be used to cover capital costs or to fund charitable activities".[a] Proton's foundation also takes on its grant-giving.[b]
representativeExamples: Proton, whose foundation is its largest voting shareholder.[b] The model's publisher lists Zeiss, Novo Nordisk, Patagonia, Bosch, Signal, Buurtzorg and Carlsberg among the companies that have implemented it.[a]
differentiationNote: Unlike a stakeholder-governed corporation, control follows the stewards, not shareholding; a company can be both. Unlike a nonprofit, it remains a for-profit company that earns and reinvests profit. Unlike a conventional corporation, its owners cannot extract the value it creates.

references.note: Purpose Foundation, "Steward ownership" (page read 21 November 2026): the model's own statement of its two principles (self-determination and purpose-orientation), that profits serve the mission and cannot be extracted by the owners, and a list of companies that have implemented it. Cited for the definition and the adopters.

Proton, announcement of the Proton Foundation (page read 21 November 2026): states that the foundation is the largest voting shareholder of Proton, that no change of control can occur without its consent, and that it takes on Proton's grant-giving. Cited as an adopter.

name: Intergovernmental Organization
primaryDefinition: "An organization established by a treaty or other instrument governed by international law and possessing its own international legal personality", which "may include as members, in addition to States, other entities", in the UN International Law Commission's 2011 draft articles.[a] The United Nations is the standard example: membership "is open to all other peace-loving states which accept the obligations contained in the present Charter".[b]
shortDescription: An organization created by a treaty among states, with states as members and its own legal personality under international law.
governanceModel: Member states decide through the organization's own bodies under its founding treaty. In the UN General Assembly "each member ... shall have one vote", and decisions on important questions are made "by a two-thirds majority of the members present and voting".[b]
legalTerritorialStatus: No territorial claim of its own. Its legal personality comes from the founding treaty under international law; the UN "shall enjoy in the territory of each of its Members such legal capacity as may be necessary for the exercise of its functions and the fulfilment of its purposes".[a][b]
membershipBasis: States join by accepting the founding treaty's obligations; the UN General Assembly admits a state on the Security Council's recommendation.[b]
fundingTreasury: "The expenses of the Organization shall be borne by the Members as apportioned by the General Assembly."[b]
differentiationNote: Unlike a nation-state, its members are states, not citizens, and its legal personality comes from a treaty, not from statehood. Unlike a nonprofit or a GAN, it is created by treaty among governments, not under a state's company or charity law or by agreement among organizations. Unlike an open-process consensus body, its rules are treaty obligations that states ratify.

references.note: UN International Law Commission, Draft articles on the responsibility of international organizations (2011), Art. 2(a): defines an international organization as one established by a treaty or other instrument governed by international law and possessing its own international legal personality. Cited for the definition.

Charter of the United Nations (full text read 21 November 2026), Arts. 4, 17, 18 and 104: membership of states that accept the Charter's obligations, expenses apportioned among Members, one vote per member and a two-thirds majority on important questions, and legal capacity in each Member's territory. Cited for the governance, membership, funding and legal status.
